componentPlan.focusQuote: The hydrologic cycle involves the continuous circulation of water in the Earth-Atmosphere system.
componentPlan.pedagogicalReason: The listed diagram shows the water cycle, so labeling parts builds location and vocabulary knowledge.

componentPlan.focusQuote: Of the many processes involved in the hydrologic cycle, the most important are:
componentPlan.pedagogicalReason: The page orders cycle stages from evaporation to runoff, so sequencing traces water movement.

overview.headline: Continuous circulation of water between ground and atmosphere

keyPoints.point: Students learn that evaporation is a change of state from liquid water that requires energy.
keyPoints.quote: Evaporation is the change of state in a substance from a liquid to a gas.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that transpiration moves water from plants through stomata to the atmosphere.
keyPoints.quote: Transpiration is the evaporation of water from plants through stomata.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that condensation changes water vapor into liquid and releases heat.
keyPoints.quote: Condensation is the process whereby water vapor is changed into a liquid state.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that precipitation falls to Earth as rain, hail, snow or sleet.
keyPoints.quote: Precipitation can be in the form of rain, hail, snow, or sleet.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that runoff occurs when excessive precipitation leaves ground saturated that cannot absorb more water.
keyPoints.quote: Runoff occurs when there is excessive precipitation and the ground is saturated (cannot absorb any more water).

keyTerms.gloss: Change of state from liquid to gas that requires energy.
keyTerms.quote: Evaporation is the change of state in a substance from a liquid to a gas.

keyTerms.gloss: Evaporation of water from plants through leaf pores.
keyTerms.quote: Transpiration is the evaporation of water from plants through stomata.

keyTerms.gloss: Small openings on leaves that release water vapor.
keyTerms.quote: Stomata are small openings found on the underside of leaves that are connected to vascular plant tissues.

keyTerms.gloss: Process where water vapor becomes liquid and releases heat.
keyTerms.quote: Condensation is the process whereby water vapor is changed into a liquid state.

keyTerms.gloss: Temperature when air becomes saturated and forms fog.
keyTerms.quote: Foggy conditions often occur when air temperature and dew point are equal.

keyTerms.gloss: Water falling to Earth as rain, hail, snow or sleet.
keyTerms.quote: Precipitation can be in the form of rain, hail, snow, or sleet.

keyTerms.gloss: Excess water flowing over saturated ground into rivers and lakes.
keyTerms.quote: Runoff occurs when there is excessive precipitation and the ground is saturated (cannot absorb any more water).

analysis.pageCoverage: The page explains the hydrologic cycle, including evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation and runoff, with everyday examples and energy exchanges.
